title: Hannah's quiet prayer (1 Samuel 1:13)
hook: Hannah's lips moved but her voice wasn't heard; the rabbis made her the model of the silent Amidah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Amidah's first words, from Psalm 51. Your line was the front door, already inside. Did the right words come when you needed them? Today, the woman who taught the rabbis how those words should sound. Day five hundred seventy-six.

Shiloh, in the days of the judges. The sanctuary is busy with families who've come for the yearly offering. One woman isn't eating. Hannah has no children, and her husband's other wife, who has several, has been needling her about it for years. She gets up, goes to the sanctuary, and prays. The old priest Eli is sitting by the doorpost, watching her. Her lips are moving. No sound is coming out. He comes to a conclusion, and it's the wrong one.
screen: `SHILOH. A WOMAN NOT EATING.` → `HER LIPS MOVE. NO SOUND.` → `THE PRIEST GETS IT WRONG.`

segments.voice: First Samuel tells it in one verse. In the old Jewish translation: Hannah "spoke in her heart; only her lips moved," but her voice couldn't be heard, and Eli thought she was drunk. He scolds her: put away your wine. And she answers with great dignity: I'm not drunk, I'm a woman in deep sorrow, pouring out my soul before the Lord. Eli changes his tune and blesses her. In time she has a son, Samuel, who grows up to be a prophet. The rabbis read this scene very closely. In Berakhot 31a, the Talmud says: how many great laws can be learned from Hannah's prayer. She spoke in her heart: so the one who prays must direct the heart. Only her lips moved: so you form the words with your lips, not only in your head. Her voice couldn't be heard: so the Amidah is said quietly, not shouted. And Eli thought she was drunk: so a drunk person shouldn't pray. Four laws from one sentence. Think about who this makes the teacher. Not a priest, not a king, not a prophet. A woman whom the priest misjudged, praying in tears, about something everyone around her had stopped asking about. And to this day, when a whole synagogue stands in near silence with lips moving, they're praying the way Hannah prayed at Shiloh. The model for the Amidah is a private conversation, mistaken for drunkenness.
screen: `SHE SPOKE IN HER HEART.` · `ELI THOUGHT SHE WAS DRUNK.` · `FOUR LAWS FROM ONE VERSE.` · `THE WHOLE ROOM PRAYS LIKE HANNAH.` · then, large: `HANNAH PRAYED QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray silently, moving your lips. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing that's heavy for you, the kind of thing you've stopped mentioning to anyone. Now say something about it, a sentence or two, with your lips moving but no sound. If you pray, you can speak it to God, the way Hannah did. If not, speak it to the quiet. Notice how different it feels from thinking. Your mouth is part of it now. The bell holds the time.
Hannah. The woman at Shiloh whose lips moved without a sound — the rabbis' model for how the Amidah, prayer of the heart, is said.
Your line: hannah prayed quietly. Today, when you notice someone praying, crying or talking to themselves, assume Hannah, not drunk. Day five hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Jews say the Amidah in a whisper, forming the words with the lips so they can hear themselves but the person beside them can't; the Talmud draws these rules from Hannah's prayer at Shiloh.

fork.setup: you're Hannah. the priest has just accused you of being drunk in the sanctuary. what do you do?
options: explain, with dignity, that you're pouring out your soul.
argue that he has no right to judge you.
fork.reveal: she tells him she's a woman in sorrow, pouring out her soul. Eli blesses her, and in time Samuel is born.

original.note: Hebrew: speaking on her heart. 1 Samuel 1:13, the root of praying from the heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old story about a woman who wanted a child.
what it means: the model for how Jews pray the Amidah: heart directed, lips moving, voice unheard.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 31a lists the laws learned from 1 Samuel 1:13, including that a drunk person may not pray.
